passages.t: After all these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib
passages.happening: ‘After all these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah. He laid siege to the fortified cities, intending to conquer them for himself’ (verse 1). Hezekiah and his officials stop up the springs outside the city, rebuild the broken wall, build an outer wall, strengthen the supporting terraces, and make weapons and shields (verses 2-5). He gathers the commanders and says, “Be strong and courageous! Do not be afraid or discouraged before the king of Assyria and the vast army with him, for there is a greater One with us than with him” (verse 7). “With him is only the arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God to help us and to fight our battles” (verse 8). The people are strengthened by his words.
passages.hearers:
The chapter opens with a pointed phrase: after all these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib came. Hezekiah's reform did not buy him an easy life; it prepared him to face the greatest army of his age. The chapter shows that trust in God is not naive: the king who seeks the LORD also builds walls and organizes defense, but he knows where his help comes from.

Sennacherib's campaign against Judah in 701 BC is one of the best documented events of the Old Testament period, told at greater length in 2 Kings 18 to 20 and Isaiah 36 to 39. His own annals, preserved on clay prisms, claim that he captured forty-six of Hezekiah's fortified cities and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem, and they record tribute from Judah, but they do not claim that Jerusalem fell. Reliefs from his palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum, show the siege and capture of Lachish. Kings also records that Hezekiah paid heavy tribute, which Chronicles leaves out.

Water was the key to surviving a siege. Stopping the springs outside denied the Assyrians water. A thick stretch of city wall uncovered in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter, often called the Broad Wall, is widely linked to Hezekiah's outer wall. Hezekiah's words echo the charge to Joshua, and the arm of flesh, basar, means merely human strength set against the LORD.
passages.later: Jeremiah used the same image: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, who makes the flesh his strength and turns his heart from the LORD’ (Jeremiah 17:5).
passages.asks: Hezekiah built walls and still told his people their strength was the LORD. Ask whether you do your part as if everything depends on it and still trust as if it does not. And ask who around you needs to hear that there is a greater One with them.

passages.t: The taunt, the prayer, and the deliverance
passages.happening:
Sennacherib, at Lachish, sends officers to Jerusalem: what is Judah trusting in, that it stays under siege (verses 9-10)? Hezekiah is misleading them, they say; no god of any nation has delivered his people from Assyria, ‘how much less will your God deliver you from my hand’ (verse 15). They shout in Hebrew to the people on the wall to frighten them, and speak of Jerusalem's God as of the gods of the peoples, the work of human hands (verses 18-19).

‘In response, King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz cried out to heaven in prayer’ (verse 20), ‘and the LORD sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor and every leader and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he withdrew to his own land in disgrace’ (verse 21), and later his own sons strike him down in the temple of his god. ‘So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from the hands of King Sennacherib of Assyria and all the others, and He gave them rest on every side’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Assyrian warfare relied on fear as much as on siege engines. Speaking to the defenders in their own language, mocking their gods and listing conquered nations were standard tactics to break a city's will. The argument rests on the old assumption that when a nation fell its god had been defeated. The Chronicler answers it: the other gods were the work of human hands, and the LORD is not one of them.

The central section is built on one verb, natsal, to deliver, which the Assyrians repeat over and over: which god has delivered, how can your God deliver. The narrator answers with a different verb: the LORD saved. Sennacherib was killed by his sons in 681 BC, some twenty years later; verse 21 compresses the interval to make the connection plain.
passages.later: Isaiah tells it this way: ‘Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (Isaiah 37:36).
passages.hard:
What happened to the Assyrian army, and why do Assyrian records not mention a disaster?

Verse 21 says the LORD sent an angel who destroyed the Assyrian commanders, and Kings and Isaiah give a large death toll. Sennacherib's annals boast of victories in Judah but say nothing of a disaster, and they do not claim that Jerusalem fell, which is unusual for a campaign ending in a siege. Ancient royal records rarely admitted defeats, so their silence is not surprising. Some historians connect the biblical account with an outbreak of disease in the camp; the Greek historian Herodotus preserves a separate tradition of an Assyrian army's sudden failure on the border of Egypt, though its relation to this event is uncertain. Others take the account as a straightforward report of a miracle. Believers read it as God's act; historians agree that Jerusalem, unlike Lachish, survived.
passages.asks: The enemy asked what Judah was trusting in. Ask what your confidence actually rests on when you are under pressure. And ask what voices on the wall are telling you that God cannot deliver you.

passages.t: Illness, pride, the water tunnel, and a test
passages.happening:
‘In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. So he prayed to the LORD, who spoke to him and gave him a sign’ (verse 24). ‘But because his heart was proud, Hezekiah did not repay the favor shown to him’ (verse 25), and wrath came on Judah and Jerusalem. ‘Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart’ (verse 26), he and the people, and the wrath did not come in his days.

He has great wealth and honor, storehouses and cities (verses 27-29). ‘It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper outlet of the Spring of Gihon and channeled it down to the west side of the City of David’ (verse 30). When envoys come from Babylon to ask about the wonder in the land, ‘God left him alone to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah’s heart’ (verse 31). His acts are written in the vision of Isaiah (verse 32), and he is buried with honor (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The ending is honest. Hezekiah, delivered and exalted, becomes proud, humbles himself, kana, and is tested again. The section compresses what Kings and Isaiah tell at length, assuming readers know those accounts and pointing them to Isaiah's vision. Hezekiah's illness is told as the occasion of his prayer and of God's sign; it is the pride that follows that brings wrath.

Hezekiah's water tunnel, cut through the rock to bring the Gihon spring inside the city to the pool of Siloam, still exists and can be walked today. An inscription found in it in 1880 describes the moment the two teams of diggers met. Envoys from distant kings were a normal part of diplomacy; 2 Kings 20 names their sender, Merodach-baladan, a Babylonian ruler resisting Assyria, and tells how Hezekiah showed them his treasures, signaling interest in an alliance. The last detail quietly introduces the power that will one day destroy Jerusalem.
passages.later: Second Kings tells the same visit: ‘At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness’ (2 Kings 20:12).
passages.asks: God left Hezekiah alone to see what was in his heart. Ask what you do when success makes you feel that you no longer need to ask. And ask what a test might show is in your heart.
